AIFs
Alternative investments

Alternative investment funds (AIFs)

What they are, how SEBI classifies them, how they compare with mutual funds and PMS, what they cost, and what you can and cannot find out before investing.

The three categoriesAIF, PMS or mutual fundWhat to askPMS ratings →

The three categories

SEBI's AIF Regulations, 2012 sort every fund into one of three categories, which decides what it may invest in, whether it may borrow and how it is taxed.

Category I

Start-ups, early-stage and social ventures, SME and infrastructure funds. Usually closed-ended, 7–10 years, money called in stages. Income passes through to investors for tax.

Category II

Private equity, private credit, real estate and funds of funds: everything that is not I or III, with no borrowing beyond day-to-day needs. Closed-ended, often 5–8 years; income passes through.

Category III

Listed-market strategies that can trade actively and use leverage or derivatives: long-only, long-short. Can be open-ended. Taxed in the fund, not in your hands.

How investing works

Most Category I and II funds work on commitments: you commit an amount, say ₹1 crore, and the fund draws it down over two to four years as it finds investments, then returns money as it exits them. Your money can be tied up for 6 to 10 years.

Who it suits

  • Investors who can commit at least ₹1 crore (₹25 lakh for the fund's own employees and directors; SEBI-accredited investors can go lower).
  • Money you will not need for the fund's whole life.
  • Portfolios already well diversified in listed markets.

Costs

Typically a management fee of 1.5–2.5% a year on committed or invested capital and a share of profits (often 10–20%) above a hurdle rate, plus set-up and operating expenses. Since 2023 SEBI requires AIFs to offer a direct plan without a distribution fee; through us, the fund pays a distribution fee, and we tell you how much before you invest.

Tax

  • Category I and II are pass-through: income is taxed in your hands as if you earned it directly (capital gains, interest, dividends), except business income, which the fund pays.
  • Category III is taxed at the fund level, often at the highest rate, so returns are reported after tax.

Risks

  • Illiquidity: you usually cannot exit early, and secondary sales are rare and at a discount.
  • Valuation: holdings are valued periodically, not daily, so reported returns can look smoother than reality.
  • Manager and strategy risk, and outcomes that can be negative.

How we help

We compare managers on their earlier funds' realised returns, not just paper gains, and on fees, strategy and fit with your portfolio. We handle the paperwork and track capital calls, distributions and reports over the fund's life.

Why we do not rank AIFs

No one publishes returns for individual AIF schemes. SEBI's benchmarking framework (CRISIL, NSE and others) gives each AIF its own report privately and publishes only category-level averages twice a year, for March and September. Private equity and credit funds are also valued only occasionally, and their returns depend on when each investment is sold. A ranking from public data would be guesswork, so we do not make one.

What to ask before investing

  • The scheme's returns since its first close, as an IRR, against its category benchmark from the benchmarking agency's report.
  • The fees: management fee, set-up costs, the hurdle rate and the manager's share of profits.
  • The lock-in and when the fund expects to return money; whether you can exit early.
  • How your returns are taxed: Category I and II pass income through to investors; Category III is taxed in the fund.

Common questions

What is the minimum investment in an AIF?

₹1 crore for most investors; ₹25 lakh for the fund's employees and directors. SEBI-accredited investors can invest less.

Can I withdraw from an AIF early?

Usually not. Category I and II funds are close-ended with a life of at least three years, often 6 to 10.

How are AIFs taxed?

Category I and II pass income through to investors, taxed in their hands; Category III pays tax at the fund level.

Are AIFs regulated?

Yes, by SEBI under the AIF Regulations, 2012. Regulation does not make them safe; it sets disclosure and conduct rules.
